patient.chief_complaint: Sudden onset difficulty speaking and right-sided weakness
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Doreen Caldwell is a 68-year-old left-handed African American woman with a history of atrial fibrillation (self-discontinued warfarin 4 months ago), poorly controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes on insulin and oral agents, HFpEF, and CKD stage 3a, who was brought by ambulance to the emergency department after her daughter called 911 when she arrived for a scheduled visit and found her mother on the living room floor. The daughter reports speaking to her mother by phone at approximately 09:00 this morning, at which time she sounded entirely normal. The daughter arrived at the home at 10:45 and found the front door unlocked. She discovered her mother sitting on the floor next to the couch, leaning against it, with her right arm limp at her side. Mrs. Caldwell was attempting to speak but her words were garbled and she appeared confused and frightened. There was no evidence of head trauma, urinary incontinence, or tongue biting. No vomiting was reported. EMS arrived at 10:58 and documented right-sided hemiparesis with facial droop and expressive aphasia. A prehospital stroke alert was activated. Prehospital fingerstick glucose was 202 mg/dL. The cardiac monitor showed an irregularly irregular rhythm without distinct P waves, consistent with atrial fibrillation. She was transported to our comprehensive stroke center with arrival at 11:22. On ED assessment, Mrs. Caldwell was alert but distressed, speaking in short effortful phrases. She was able to state her name but could not reliably provide her birthdate or describe what happened. Her daughter confirmed that the last known well time was 09:00, making the symptom duration approximately 2 hours and 22 minutes at time of ED arrival, well within the thrombolytic treatment window. Her daughter also confirmed that Mrs. Caldwell stopped taking warfarin approximately four months ago because she was developing large bruises on her arms and was worried about falling and bleeding.

output.query: acute ischemic stroke atrial fibrillation anticoagulation timing guidelines

results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: For patients with AF-related stroke, initiation of oral anticoagulation is recommended, but optimal timing depends on stroke severity and risk of hemorrhagic transformation. Most experts recommend starting anticoagulation 4-14 days after stroke onset.

results.title: Timing of Oral Anticoagulant Therapy in Acute Ischemic Stroke With Atrial Fibrillation (ELAN Trial)
results.key_finding: Early initiation of DOACs (within 48 hours for minor strokes, within 6-7 days for moderate strokes) was noninferior to later initiation with respect to a composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, major extracranial bleeding, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, or vascular death at 30 days.

results.title: European Stroke Organisation guidelines on antithrombotic treatment after stroke
results.key_finding: For patients with AF and moderate ischemic stroke (NIHSS 8-15), anticoagulation may be started at day 6-7. For severe stroke (NIHSS >=16), consider starting at day 12-14 after repeat imaging to exclude hemorrhagic transformation.

output.summary: Current evidence supports initiating oral anticoagulation (preferably a DOAC) in AF-related ischemic stroke patients. Timing depends on stroke severity: minor strokes (NIHSS <8) may start within 48 hours, moderate strokes within 6-7 days, and severe strokes at 12-14 days after exclusion of hemorrhagic transformation on repeat imaging. The ELAN trial demonstrated that earlier DOAC initiation was non-inferior to delayed initiation with respect to a composite of recurrent ischemic events, major bleeding, and vascular death at 30 days.

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast head CT MUST exclude intracranial hemorrhage before IV thrombolysis is considered (tPA decision modeled here through drug-interaction/contraindication check).
Glucose, INR/PTT, and platelet count must be reviewed before IV thrombolysis to exclude hypoglycemia mimic and coagulopathy contraindications.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Begin secondary prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) and high-intensity statin per mechanism
Lower BP to <185/110 mmHg with IV labetalol or nicardipine BEFORE administering IV tPA
After tPA, maintain BP <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours
If no tPA, permissive hypertension up to ~220/110 mmHg may be acceptable to preserve penumbral perfusion
Adjust contrast use for CKD stage 3a
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not administer IV tPA with BP >185/110 mmHg
Do not lower BP rapidly below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase
Do not delay anticoagulation indefinitely after acute window passes

Avoid order_ct_scan with contrast=True, angiography=True: Iodinated contrast carries nephrotoxicity risk in CKD stage 3a — pre-hydrate and consider MR angiography alternative if dissection or other cause requires further characterization
key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Stroke-related BP elevation is initially adaptive; pre-tPA target is <185/110, post-tPA <180/105
AF off anticoagulation with HFpEF and CKD is a high-recurrence-risk profile requiring anticoagulation
Hypertensive emergency does not equal hemorrhagic stroke — neuroimaging defines the lesion
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup

clinical_pearls: African Americans have nearly twice the rate of first stroke compared to white Americans, partly attributable to higher prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, and obesity
Self-discontinuation of anticoagulation is a common real-world problem; approximately 30% of AF patients discontinue OAC within the first year
Left-handedness does not reliably predict right-hemisphere language dominance; over 70% of left-handed individuals are still left-hemisphere dominant for language
CKD stage 3a requires monitoring but does not contraindicate standard-dose apixaban unless additional dose-reduction criteria are met (age >=80, weight <=60 kg, Cr >=1.5)
